subject: radiology
title: Embolisation agents and techniques

steps.tx: Embolic agents are chosen by how long the vessel must stay blocked. **Gelfoam** is a temporary agent that reopens within weeks and suits trauma and nosebleeds that heal. Permanent agents include coils, plugs, particles and **calibrated microspheres** for tumour and fibroid beds. **Liquid agents** such as glue cast the vessel itself and reach feeders that catheters cannot enter. Matching duration to disease avoids both rebleeding and needless tissue infarction.
steps.say: Embolic agents are chosen by how long the vessel must stay blocked. Gelfoam is temporary and reopens within weeks as tissues heal. Coils and particles block permanently and suit tumours and fibroids well. Liquid agents are valuable because they cast the vessel and reach difficult feeders safely.

steps.tx: Bleeding embolisation follows the vessel directly to the bleeding source. Brisk upper gastrointestinal bleeding beyond endoscopy is closed with **mesenteric coils** after angiographic localisation. **Splenic embolisation** preserves the spleen in blunt trauma with a blush or high grade injury. Massive haemoptysis in tuberculosis usually arises from hypertrophied **bronchial arteries** that are embolised first. Severe nosebleeds that fail packing are treated through internal maxillary and facial branches.
steps.say: Bleeding embolisation follows the vessel directly to the bleeding source. Gut bleeding beyond endoscopy is closed with coils after localisation. Splenic embolisation is valuable because it preserves the spleen in blunt trauma cases. Massive haemoptysis usually arises from bronchial arteries, and severe nosebleeds are treated through maxillary branches after packing fails.

steps.tx: The left angiogram shows a dark pool of **active gastrointestinal bleeding** arising from a mesenteric feeder beyond endoscopic reach. The inset shows the same feeder packed with a **mesenteric coil** and complete contrast stasis beyond it. Normal neighbouring branches remain open while the bleeding branch is closed securely. This before and after pair teaches the **stasis endpoint** that examiners expect for bleeding embolisation.
steps.say: The left angiogram shows active gut bleeding that arises from a mesenteric feeder. The inset shows the feeder packed with coils and complete stasis beyond. Neighbouring branches remain open while the bleeding branch is closed. This pair teaches the stasis endpoint that examiners expect after bleeding embolisation.

steps.tx: Every embolisation balances benefit against the risk of tissue loss. **Post embolisation syndrome** with fever, pain and nausea follows tumour work and needs fluids and analgesia. **Non target embolisation** is the feared error, so a **microcatheter** tip sits beyond normal branches before release. A migrated coil can infarct downstream tissue, while very small particles may pass through a shunt into the lungs. Abscess can complicate a necrotic embolised tumour and needs follow up imaging.
steps.say: Every embolisation is a balance between benefit gained and risk of tissue loss. Fever with pain after tumour work usually reflects ischaemia and needs fluids. Non target embolisation is the feared error and needs careful catheter positioning. A migrated coil can infarct tissue, while tiny particles may pass through a shunt into the lungs.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating superselective microcatheter placement beyond normal branches to prevent non-target embolisation during therapeutic procedures, showing embolic agent release.
vis.caption: Superselective microcatheter placement prevents non-target embolisation of normal vessels

steps.tx: The chosen endpoint decides whether embolisation has succeeded or failed. **Stasis** in the target feeder with preserved flow in normal vessels marks complete bleeding control. Tumour success is judged by loss of abnormal **tumour blush** rather than by the number of coils used. Pain relief after musculoskeletal embolisation takes weeks, so early imaging should not trigger retreatment. **Rebleeding** within days usually means a missed collateral or reopened temporary agent.
steps.say: The chosen endpoint decides whether embolisation has succeeded or failed. Stasis in the target feeder with normal flow preserved marks complete control. Tumour success is judged by loss of blush rather than coil numbers. Pain relief takes weeks after musculoskeletal work, and early rebleeding usually means a missed collateral vessel.
